mcqs.question: A class `OrderValidator` has three methods — `checkStock()`, `checkAddress()`, `checkPayment()` — all of which change only when the rules for "is this order valid" change. Does this violate SRP?
options: No — all three methods serve the same responsibility, so there's still only one reason to change
Yes — SRP requires every class to have exactly one method
Yes — three methods automatically means three responsibilities
It depends only on how many lines of code the class has
mcqs.explanation: SRP counts reasons to change, not methods. Because all three methods change for the same underlying reason (validation rules changing), this class is single-responsibility even with multiple methods. SRP never mandates a one-method limit, and method count alone doesn't determine responsibility count.

mcqs.question: In the `Invoice` class that mixes `calculateTotal()`, `saveToDatabase()`, and `formatAsPdfText()`, what's the concrete risk of leaving it unsplit?
options: The class becomes slower at runtime because it has more methods
A change to how PDFs are formatted could accidentally break pricing or persistence code compiled in the same class
Java won't allow a class to have both persistence and formatting methods
The class will fail to compile once it exceeds three methods
mcqs.explanation: The real risk of an unsplit SRP violation is coupling unrelated changes: touching formatting code sits in the same file as pricing and persistence logic, raising the chance of an accidental regression when only one concern was meant to change. Method count doesn't affect runtime speed or compilation.

mcqs.question: A team split a `ReportGenerator` class into eight tiny classes, but every code review still touches all eight together for any report change. What does this suggest?
options: The split was correct and should be extended even further
The eight classes were never separate responsibilities — they should likely be merged back
SRP has been fully achieved and no further action is needed
The team should add unit tests before deciding anything
mcqs.explanation: Classes that always change together for the same reason were never separate responsibilities in the SRP sense — over-splitting just scatters one true reason-to-change across many files. That's a sign to merge them back, not to split further or declare success.

mcqs.question: How does high cohesion relate to the Single Responsibility Principle?
options: They're unrelated — cohesion is about performance, SRP is about testing
High cohesion is the opposite of SRP; a class should aim for one but not the other
A highly cohesive class — where every member serves one purpose — naturally tends to have one reason to change
Cohesion only applies to functions, never to classes
mcqs.explanation: Cohesion and SRP describe the same underlying quality from different angles: when every field and method in a class serves a single purpose, there's naturally only one reason for that class to change. They aren't opposites, aren't unrelated, and cohesion applies at the class level too.
